reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant late-onset distal myopathy caused by variants in ZASP (encoded by LDB3), a Z-disc protein, and classified within the myofibrillar myopathies
Onset is typically after the fourth or fifth decade, with distal weakness commonly beginning in the lower legs, and both anterior and posterior compartment involvement may occur
As a myofibrillar myopathy it may be accompanied by cardiomyopathy, cardiac conduction disease, and peripheral neuropathy, so cardiac and neurological assessment is important
Weakness gradually extends to more proximal muscles over time, but progression is generally slow
Creatine kinase is normal or mildly to moderately elevated and electromyography shows myopathic changes, sometimes with irritable or neurogenic-appearing features
Muscle biopsy shows the myofibrillar pathology hallmark of Z-disc streaming with abnormal accumulation of proteins such as desmin and myotilin, often with rimmed vacuoles
The ZASP/LDB3 gene overlaps phenotypically with other myofibrillar myopathy genes, so a broad panel is often needed
Diagnosis integrates the distal myopathy pattern, myofibrillar biopsy features, and LDB3 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Markesbery-Griggs myopathy is a myofibrillar myopathy caused by dominant variants in LDB3, which encodes the Z-band alternatively spliced PDZ-motif protein (ZASP). ZASP stabilises the sarcomeric Z-disc through interactions with alpha-actinin and other cytoskeletal proteins. Mutant ZASP disrupts Z-disc integrity, leading to disintegration of myofibrils, streaming of Z-disc material, and abnormal aggregation of cytoskeletal proteins including desmin. This myofibrillar disorganisation produces progressive muscle weakness and, because the same proteins are important in cardiac muscle and nerve, predisposes to associated cardiomyopathy, conduction disease, and neuropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Other myofibrillar myopathies (desmin, myotilin, filamin C, BAG3, crystallin-related)
Chronic acquired neuropathy contributing to distal weakness
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for desmin, myotilin, and other myofibrillar markers
Muscle MRI to map the pattern of involvement
Cardiac evaluation with ECG and echocardiography given the myofibrillar cardiac risk
Genetic testing with an LDB3-inclusive myofibrillar myopathy panel
redFlags: Cardiomyopathy or conduction block requiring cardiac monitoring and possible device therapy
Respiratory muscle weakness with declining vital capacity
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative or overlapping diagnosis
New arrhythmia or syncope in a patient or affected relative
reference.prognosis: Skeletal muscle weakness progresses slowly over years, but overall prognosis depends heavily on associated cardiac involvement; unrecognised cardiomyopathy or conduction disease can be life-limiting, making cardiac surveillance central to management.
pitfalls: Failing to screen for and monitor the cardiac complications typical of myofibrillar myopathies
Misdiagnosing it as inclusion body myositis on the basis of rimmed vacuoles alone
Relying on a narrow genetic test rather than a broad myofibrillar panel given phenotypic overlap
Overlooking respiratory involvement in later disease
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
